grammar.title: Frase
grammar.rule: Muitas tarefas, poucas pessoas. Mais pessoas, menos tarefas para Ana.
grammar.note_en:
This chapter uses numbers to make real choices: how many books two people can carry, how many books that would provide, and how a chair layout keeps the exit clear. The number words six through twenty are seis, sete, oito, nove, dez, onze, doze, treze, catorze, quinze, dezesseis, dezessete, dezoito, dezenove, vinte. The numerical margin reference pairs each word with its written numeral before it is reused. Catorze is the form used here; quatorze is an equally standard spelling accepted wherever that number is keyed. Brazilian dezesseis, dezessete and dezenove keep the same spellings throughout this course.

A cardinal number tells how many. Six books is seis livros; six chairs is seis cadeiras. Numbers from three to twenty in this chapter do not change for a masculine or feminine noun. The earlier one/two distinction still matters: um livro, uma cadeira (“one book, one chair”), dois livros, duas cadeiras (“two books, two chairs”). The noun is plural after quantities greater than one: quinze livros (“fifteen books”), vinte cadeiras (“twenty chairs”). Um dia / dois dias means “one day / two days”: dia ends in -a but is masculine. Uma tarefa / duas tarefas means “one task / two tasks”: tarefa is feminine. The written chair labels are identifiers, not new ordinal forms: cadeira quinze is “chair fifteen,” the position marked15 on the plan, not a lesson on how to form ‘fifteenth’.

Muito and pouco express quantity. When they determine a noun they agree with that noun in gender and number. Muito espaço means “much/a lot of space”; muitos papéis, “many papers”; muitas tarefas, “many tasks.” Pouco café means “little coffee”; poucas pessoas, “few people”; poucas mesas, “few tables.” English may prefer “a lot of” to “much” in an affirmative sentence, but the Portuguese noun still determines the form. Espaço and café in these uses are treated as an amount; papers, tasks and people are counted as plural items. This chapter’s table shows the forms actually read; it does not introduce an unseen four-cell paradigm or an adverbial rule. The story’s pouco café is a small amount of coffee, not a judgment that the drink is bad.

Mais and menos do not agree with the noun: mais pessoas means “more people,” menos tarefas means “fewer tasks.” Mais um livro means “one more book”; menos tarefas para Ana means “fewer tasks for Ana.” Do not give mais or menos a plural ending. They state an increase or decrease relative to the situation under discussion. This chapter does not teach the later comparative construction with que, or all uses of muito as an adverb.

A lista tem nove tarefas means “The list has nine tasks.” The infinitives in the written list name actions: tirar papéis (“remove papers”), limpar o chão (“clean the floor”), colocar mesas/cadeiras (“put tables/chairs in place”), levar livros (“carry books”), preparar café (“prepare coffee”), escrever nomes (“write names”), mostrar o caminho (“show the route”), abrir a entrada (“open the entrance”). Action labels on the list are not newly introduced finite commands. The new infinitive limpar first appears on that list with a delivered cleaning aid and is later used after the taught modals. A task assignment does not mean the job has already been completed. The shipment and cleaning remain uncompleted at the end.

Amanhã means “tomorrow,” the day after the day of speaking. Sábado names Saturday. Amanhã é sábado means “Tomorrow is Saturday”; amanhã is not itself a verb tense. Here the calendar locates the current day immediately to the left of the labelled Saturday, so the scene is on Friday, without requiring a new Portuguese weekday word. O dia da noite com livros means “the day of the evening with books”: dia refers to the calendar day that includes the evening, not only daylight. No sábado means “on Saturday”; the already known em + o gives no. Rosa pode levar seu livro amanhã means “Rosa can bring her book tomorrow.” The present modal pode with a time expression describes her ability/commitment in context; it does not introduce ir + infinitive future, a later target.

Read the count as a plan rather than a delivery record. Fifteen promised market books plus the three existing café books make eighteen planned books. Rosa’s offered book makes nineteen; the male neighbor’s makes twenty. The alternate carrying estimates give sixteen or seventeen, but are rejected because they remove needed workers from the café/courtyard. The ten chair positions from existing stock and ten promised chairs are drawn on paper; no twenty chairs have appeared by magic. The two names and the still-empty number field at the end set up the next chapter’s scheduling problem. Clock figures like20:00 are recognizable written records already seen in the old notebook, not a new lesson on telling time; no spoken hour construction is required in this chapter.
